title: Multivariate Quantum Signal Processing
abstract: We develop Multivariate Quantum Signal Processing for designing matrix-valued transformations of multiple noncommuting nonnormal block-encoded matrices. Our framework equips quantum transducers with the analytic structure of multiport Infinite-Impulse-Response (IIR) filters and establishes a transfer-function methodology for designing quantum query algorithms. Efficiently computable analytic bounds that hold uniformly across the oracle promise yield efficient quantum circuits with logarithmic error dependence and near-unity success probability, paralleling the approximation-theoretic guarantees of univariate QSP/QSVT. We provide a complete characterization of achievable transfer functions and a principled library of analytic IIR components. Our modular designs greatly improve or resolve the per-oracle query complexity of open multi-oracle problems: (1) Hamiltonian simulation under $H=\sum_j H_j$ with weighted quasinorm cost $\approx t\langle\vecλ,\vec C\rangle_{1/2}+\mathcal{O}(\|\vec C\|_1\log(1/ε))$ for block-encoding normalizations $\vecλ$ and costs $\vec C$; (2) sparse simulation with optimal time--norm $Θ(\sqrt{d}\|H\|_{\rm 1\to2}t)$ and additive error dependence; (3) solving linear systems and (4) differential equations under minimal matrix assumptions with optimal weighted state-preparation and multi-term cost; (5) ground-state preparation and energy estimation; (6) generalized eigenvalue problems. We apply these to exactly simulate downfolded Hamiltonians with leading cost $t\langle\vecλ_{\rm eff},\vec C_{\rm eff}\rangle_{1/2}$ further reduced by fractional dynamic correlation energy contributions from coarse-grained Hamiltonians, and show similar classical-data-input-reduction results for multiscale graph classification via Kron reduction. We also show the online generalization with anisotropic Kalman filtering of streaming quantum data.
summary: This work introduces Multivariate Quantum Signal Processing (MQSP), a powerful framework that models quantum query algorithms using the mathematical structure of multiport IIR filters. It achieves optimal resource bounds for complex tasks like Hamiltonian simulation and solving linear equations by providing a systematic design methodology. This advances quantum algorithm design by bridging classical signal processing theory with quantum computation theory.
main_problem: The paper develops Multivariate Quantum Signal Processing (MQSP) to design efficient quantum algorithms for matrix-valued transformations involving multiple noncommuting, nonnormal matrices.
main_result: It provides a complete characterization of achievable quantum transfer functions and achieves optimal query complexity bounds for various problems, including Hamiltonian simulation and solving linear systems.
method: The core method maps quantum query algorithms onto the analytic structure of multiport Infinite-Impulse-Response (IIR) filters, using a transfer-function methodology derived from feedback loops.
model_or_system: The framework applies to quantum transducers implementing transformations defined by multiple noncommuting, nonnormal block-encoded matrices, generalizing concepts from standard Quantum Signal Processing (QSP).
key_observables: Weighted query cost, time-norm dependence, and error bounds ($\epsilon$).
important_parameters: The number of noncommuting matrices ($m$), the approximation depth ($N$), and the query cost structure ($\langle\vec\lambda,\vec Cangle_{1/2}$).
main_assumptions: The method relies on the existence of analytic IIR representations for the required transformations and involves approximating continuous IIR functions with finite-impulse-response (FIR) circuits.
paper_structure: The paper builds upon the mathematical framework of IIR filters to characterize quantum query algorithms, providing specific, optimized bounds and constructions for Hamiltonian simulation, linear system solving, and generalized eigenvalue problems.
why_interesting: The connection between classical signal processing theory (IIR filters) and quantum query complexity provides a powerful, structured, and analytically rigorous toolset for designing quantum algorithms, particularly for open quantum systems dynamics.

figures.caption: Figure 1: One oracle port with delay r = 2 and horizon N = 5. At each time, the system matrix couples the corresponding public clock subspace to one private position. These subspaces are |k⟩clk ⊗P and |k mod 2⟩j ⊗Lj. Each oracle rectangle denotes a controlled call on both private positions. The calls occur at times 2 and 4, before the corresponding system operation. An amplitude written at time k is read at k + 2 after one oracle call. The lines denote direct-sum subspaces represented by the binary address register. The input consists of the public amplitudes (u0, . . . , u4) and two initial private amplitudes. The output consists of (y0, . . . , y4) and both unmeasured private amplitudes....

Figure 2: Circuit for quditization on the binary address register and clock label. The system operation S(k) acts through the embedding Jk in Equation (2.25), coupling the indicated public and private basis subspaces. Routing updates the address during these couplings. The operation Qk applies the scheduled oracles to all their private positions. A port is scheduled precisely when rj | k. Projecting the encoding register onto |0⟩a after input-clock preparation and output-clock unpreparation gives eGN/αclk, as defined in Equations (2.32) and (A.16).

Figure 3: Examples of shared processing modules. An arrow points from a construction to a module it uses. Shaded boxes name the algorithms and their modules; all module names link to their definitions. The dashed edge denotes the weighted version of the same Cayley transformation. Elementary connections are shown in the later IIR diagrams.

Figure 4: The same tap and preparation reflection define an IIR and a finite preparation algorithm. The lift receives the prepared state in its private subspace, initially empty public slots retain every transmitted amplitude, and the final success flag selects their direct sum.

Figure 5: The sign lattice is a path of unitary sections. The two endpoints are public. A known boundary swap closes every internal coordinate, and the feedback connection applies the even and odd matchings. The marker z counts a whole two-query round.
